reading.body:
AI litigation in United States courts is tracked as living docket pages, but the data records no case count, so the volume of active suits is not stated here.

The structure of the coverage is the useful part. Cases are sorted into claim families: copyright, right of publicity, product liability and wrongful death, hiring discrimination, biometric privacy, securities fraud, trade secrets, platform access, patent, consumer protection, and government contracts. That spread matters because it shows AI disputes are not one legal story. A copyright suit over training data and a wrongful death suit over a chatbot's output reach the same technology through entirely different doctrines, and each will produce its own record and its own remedies.

The second strand is precedent. Current copyright, scraping and defamation cases are argued out of a small set of decisions made long before generative models existed: Sony on substantial non-infringing use, Campbell and Google Books on transformative purpose, Van Buren and hiQ on scraping, Zeran on Section 230. The defenses are therefore being assembled from analogies rather than from AI-specific law, and the profiles note where each analogy is weakest. That is where outcomes will turn.

What the data does not contain is any count of cases, any named party, any ruling, or any date beyond the refresh timestamps. It describes the tracking apparatus and the precedent set, not the state of any dispute. Nothing here connects to compute, buildings, or power, and no such link should be read into it.
